title: Edge Delivery block development
text:
# Edge Delivery block development

## What a block is

In Edge Delivery Services (EDS), a block is the unit of reusable functionality and styling. Authors create it in a document as a table whose first cell holds the block name. The platform converts that table into semantic HTML, and your code decorates it in the browser.

## Folder structure

Each block lives in its own folder under `blocks/`:

```
blocks/
  cards/
    cards.js
    cards.css
```

The folder name, the JavaScript file and the CSS file must share the same name. The block name from the authoring table is lowercased and hyphenated, so "Hero Banner" maps to `hero-banner`.

## The decorate function

Every block exports a default `decorate` function that receives the block element:

- Do not depend on a build step; plain CSS and modern JavaScript modules are enough.

## Variants

Authors add variants in parentheses after the block name, such as "Cards (dark, wide)". Each variant becomes a class on the block element, so `.cards.dark` can restyle it without a new block.

## Loading behavior

The page is loaded in three phases: eager (the LCP content), lazy (the rest of the page) and delayed (third-party tools such as analytics and consent). Place blocks that contain the largest image or heading above the fold and avoid adding scripts to the eager phase.

## Content-first mindset

Design the authoring model before the code. A good block has a small number of columns and rows that authors can understand without documentation. Prefer plain text, links and images over custom fields.

## Testing and linting

## Testing and linting

- Run the linter (ESLint and Stylelint) before every pull request.
- Test with the local dev server pointing at real content.
- Check Lighthouse on a branch preview; the target is a score of 100 on mobile.
- Review the block with keyboard navigation and a screen reader.

## Common pitfalls

1. Rewriting the DOM so heavily that authors' content is lost.
2. Loading fonts or libraries from the block instead of the delayed phase.
3. Adding block-specific global CSS that leaks into other blocks.
4. Skipping a fallback for missing images or empty rows.

title: CMS migration checklist
text:
# CMS migration checklist

A migration succeeds or fails on preparation. Use this checklist as a starting point and adapt it to your platform, content volume and governance model.

## 1. Discovery and inventory

- Export a full URL list from the current CMS, sitemap and analytics.
- Classify pages by template, traffic, last-modified date and owner.
- Identify content that is duplicated, outdated or legally required.
- Record integrations: search, forms, commerce, CRM, consent, analytics and SSO.

## 2. Content strategy

- Decide what to migrate, what to rewrite and what to retire.
- A common rule of thumb: retire anything with no traffic and no business purpose for twelve months.
- Define the target content model: page types, reusable blocks and metadata fields.
- Agree on naming, folder structure and URL conventions.

## 3. URL and SEO plan

## 3. URL and SEO plan

- Map every old URL to a new URL or an explicit 410.
- Prepare a redirect file and test it in bulk before go-live.
- Preserve titles, descriptions, canonical tags and structured data.
- Keep hreflang annotations consistent across language versions.
- Plan a new XML sitemap and submit it after launch.

## 4. Technical migration

- Choose an import approach: scripted conversion, manual copy for key pages, or a hybrid.
- Normalize HTML: remove inline styles, deprecated tags and tracking leftovers.
- Move media to the new DAM or content store and keep alt text.
- Validate that internal links point to the new structure rather than the legacy domain.

## 5. Governance and people

- Name a content owner for every section.
- Train authors on the new authoring experience before cutover.
- Define publishing workflows, approvals and roles.
- Document escalation paths for launch week.

## 6. Quality assurance

- Compare a sample of pages visually and structurally against the original.
- Run link, accessibility and performance checks automatically.
- Verify forms, search and integrations end to end.
- Test consent banners and analytics tags on the new pages.

## 7. Cutover

- Freeze content changes in the legacy CMS for an agreed window.
- Lower DNS TTL in advance, and keep a rollback plan.
- Launch during a low-traffic period with the team on call.
- Monitor errors, 404s and Core Web Vitals in the first 72 hours.

| Risk | Mitigation |
| --- | --- |
| Lost SEO equity | Complete redirect map, early crawl tests |
| Scope creep | Fixed template list and change control |
| Author resistance | Early training and quick wins |
| Hidden integrations | Inventory based on network traces, not only documentation |

title: Consent and analytics basics
text:
# Consent and analytics basics

## Why consent comes first

Analytics and personalization tools process personal data, such as identifiers, IP addresses and behavioral events. In the EU and UK, the ePrivacy rules and the GDPR generally require informed, prior consent before non-essential cookies or similar technologies are set. Other regions have their own rules, so confirm requirements with legal counsel.

## Categories of tracking

- **Strictly necessary:** session handling, load balancing, security. No consent needed.
- **Preferences:** language or layout choices.
- **Analytics:** measuring traffic and behavior.
- **Marketing:** advertising, retargeting and cross-site profiles.

Map each tag on your site to one of these categories and document the purpose.

## A consent management platform (CMP)

title: Consent and analytics basics
text:

Map each tag on your site to one of these categories and document the purpose.

## A consent management platform (CMP)

A CMP shows the banner, stores the visitor's choices and exposes them to your code. Good practice:

- Make "Reject" as easy as "Accept".
- Do not preselect optional categories.
- Store a timestamp and a policy version with each decision.
- Let visitors change their choice at any time through a persistent link.

## Gating tags

The rule is simple: no consent, no tag. Implement it with a tag manager or an event-driven approach:

1. Load only the CMP and essential code initially.
2. Listen for the consent event.
3. When the analytics category is granted, load the analytics library.
4. When it is revoked, stop sending events and clear related cookies where possible.

text:
en the analytics category is granted, load the analytics library.
4. When it is revoked, stop sending events and clear related cookies where possible.

On performance-focused platforms, load the CMP early enough to avoid a flash of unconsented tracking, but keep analytics in the delayed phase to protect Core Web Vitals.

## Consent Mode and modeled data

Some analytics tools support signalling consent state and use aggregated or modeled data when consent is denied. This can reduce reporting gaps, but it does not replace the need to respect the visitor's choice. Check the vendor's current documentation.

## Measurement design

title: Consent and analytics basics
text:
uce reporting gaps, but it does not replace the need to respect the visitor's choice. Check the vendor's current documentation.

## Measurement design

- Define a measurement plan with business questions first, then events.
- Use a consistent naming convention, for example `object_action` such as `form_submit`.
- Keep a data layer or event schema documented and versioned.
- Avoid sending personal data (emails, names) as event parameters.

## Data minimization and retention

Collect only what you need. Set retention periods in the analytics tool, anonymize IP addresses where supported, and review access regularly.

## Server-side considerations

Moving tags server-side can improve control and performance, but it does not remove the legal need for consent. Treat it as an architecture choice, not a compliance shortcut.

## Testing checklist

- Accept, then verify events fire as expected.
- Reject or withdraw, then verify requests stop.
- Test on mobile and with ad blockers enabled.
- Re-test after every banner or tag change.

title: Personalization with Target
text:
# Personalization with Adobe Target

## Purpose

Personalization adapts content to the visitor's context, while experimentation measures whether the change helps. Adobe Target supports both: A/B tests, experience targeting (XT), automated personalization and recommendations.

## Core concepts

- **Activity:** the test or personalization campaign.
- **Experience:** a variant shown to a segment of visitors.
- **Audience:** rules that define who qualifies, such as device, geography or a profile attribute.
- **Mbox / decision scope:** a named location where Target decides what to show.
- **Metric:** the goal, such as clicks, form submissions or revenue.

## Client-side and server-side delivery

title: Personalization with Target
text:
ation where Target decides what to show.
- **Metric:** the goal, such as clicks, form submissions or revenue.

## Client-side and server-side delivery

With the Web SDK or at.js, Target can modify the page in the browser. This is flexible but risks flicker if the page renders before the decision arrives. Server-side or edge-based decisioning avoids flicker and fits well with fast static delivery, at the cost of more engineering.

Prefer decisions that return structured content (JSON) rather than raw HTML. Your code then renders the offer using approved components.

## Avoiding flicker and performance loss

- Apply the decision to content below the fold whenever possible.
- Do not personalize the largest contentful element unless you must.
- Use a short timeout and fall back to default content.
- Keep the personalization script out of the critical path.

## Audiences that work

text:

- Use a short timeout and fall back to default content.
- Keep the personalization script out of the critical path.

## Audiences that work

Start simple:

1. New versus returning visitors.
2. Traffic source or campaign parameter.
3. Logged-in status or account tier supplied by your own systems.
4. Role or interest, inferred from explicit choices rather than guesses.

More complex, behavior-based models need enough traffic and clean data.

## Experiment hygiene

- Write a hypothesis: "Changing X for Y will improve Z because..."
- Pick one primary metric before launching.
- Calculate sample size and run for full business cycles, usually at least two weeks.
- Do not stop early because of a promising trend.
- Document the outcome, including failed tests.

## Consent and privacy

## Consent and privacy

Personalization based on identifiers or behavior generally requires consent. When consent is missing, show the default experience. Do not store sensitive attributes in profiles or send them to Target.

## Governance

Create a naming convention for activities and audiences, assign owners and retire old activities. A quarterly review keeps the library clean and avoids conflicting experiences.

## Quick start checklist

- Consent signal available before Target runs.
- Default content defined for every personalized location.
- Metrics and audiences agreed with stakeholders.
- QA performed on all variants and devices.
- Rollback procedure documented.
